utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Before the next witness is being brought in, I would like to raise some matters. Again, one decision -- one guidance related to exhibits pursuant to Rule 92 ter. In connection with a large number of exhibits tendered in association with Mr. Erdemovic's testimony last week, you will recall, Mr. McCloskey, the Chamber would like to further clarify the procedure to be followed when tendering exhibits associated with prior testimony under Rule 92 ter. In the original Rule 92 ter decision of the 3rd of November last year, again on 18th of March this year, and again on the 22nd of April, 2010, the Chamber has emphasised to the parties that the Chamber draws a distinction between the exhibits submitted with Rule 92 ter motion which were first admitted through the relevant witness in the prior proceeding, secondly used with the relevant witness, but admitted through a different witness in the prior proceeding, and, thirdly, used with the relevant witness, but ultimately not admitted in the prior proceeding. Because the Chamber employs a different approach with respect to each of these categories of proposed exhibits, it is imperative that the parties indicate on the list of exhibits, which is circulated prior to the witness appearance, to which category each proposed exhibit belongs. For those exhibits which are admitted through the witness in the prior proceeding, the Chamber considers that they are necessarily associated with the prior testimony, forming an integral part thereof, and will not require an additional showing from the tendering party. Where there are more than five such exhibits, in order to save court time, the Chamber would like the tendering party to liaise with the Registry rather than reading each exhibit into the record individually. And, Mr. McCloskey, I'm sure you will appreciate this approach. The Registry will then create an internal memorandum indicating which exhibit numbers will be assigned to each of these proposed exhibits once the witness appears in court and attests that the transcript accurately reflects the witness declaration and what the witness would say if examined pursuant to the terms of Rule 92 ter. Once the witness makes this attestation, and assuming there were no objections from the opposing party at that time, all exhibits admitted through the witness during his or her testimony in the prior proceeding will be admitted in the current case, and the Court Officer will file the memorandum in the case record. For those exhibits which were not admitted through the witness in the prior proceeding, the Chamber will require an additional showing of relevance in relation to the present case prior to admitting such exhibits. Accordingly, it is imperative that the list circulated by the tendering party prior to the witness's appearance in court clearly indicate to which category the proposed exhibits belong. Additionally, by creating a procedure to deal with large numbers of exhibits associated with prior testimony by liaising with the Registry, it is hoped that less time will need to be devoted to dealing with such administrative issues during court. I hope this guidance clarifies the situation for our future witnesses. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was just going to say, yes, I think it does. And for Mr. Erdemovic, the ones I read, those had been admitted through him in his previous testimony. That's why I didn't ask him about it, but that's -- all of those fit that category, just so you know, and we will, of course, tell you from now on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to deal with one exhibit we have discussed last week. It is D42, marked for identification. On the 17th of March, 2010, the Defence tendered the document 1D00119 as an exhibit. After having received the Prosecution's objection, the Chamber postponed the decision thereon. The document was marked for identification as D42, marked MFI. It is an interview with a person named Pelemis, published in a newspaper. The witness Drazen Erdemovic is mentioned in this interview and testified about the content of the interview and the person in question. The Chamber will receive the document, which becomes now Exhibit D42. In connection with the evidence of Witness Erdemovic, the interview has probative value. However, the Chamber is not admitting it for the truth of its content. The third matter I would like to raise is the following: The Chamber would like to provide the parties with a short explanation with respect to their positions which we have received informally on the public redacted version of our decision that was filed confidentially on the 28th of April, 2010. This decision concerned the role of Mr. Gajic in the courtroom. Having considered these positions, the Chamber has decided to redact only paragraphs 13, 14, and 15, as well as footnote 50 of the decision, on the basis that they reveal what may be considered private or personal information concerning Mr. Gajic. Having carefully reviewed the remainder of the decision, the Chamber is not of the position that there is a legitimate reason for the redaction of any further paragraphs. Paragraph 30, which the Defence submits should be redacted, does not contain any information not already contained in other portions of the decision which the Defence does not seek to have redacted. It also does not contain either private or personal information which would justify such a redaction. The public redacted version of the decision will be issued shortly. The last matter is the following: Next Monday, the 7th of June, 2010, a plenary meeting of the Judges of this Tribunal is scheduled for 1.00 p.m. It is expected to last around two hours. Therefore, we have to delay the start of our hearing that day for one hour, and will commence at 3.15 p.m. These were the preliminary matters the Chamber wanted to raise. Is there anything else? Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Your Honours, good morning. We now have a B/C/S translation for the Erdemovic plea agreement, which was P00219, and that's in e-court, so it should be okay to offer into evidence now. And Mr. Gajic just reminded us of the US letter about aerial imagery, 65 ter 6277, P214, did not have a B/C/S translation, so we are sending that for translation immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue, we will receive the -- just a moment. P219 is already an exhibit, or was it marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was marked for identification because it did not have a B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. It will now be received as an exhibit, P219. And the other -- the letter of the United States is already marked for identification? I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and we should have a translation for you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, as you're aware, we are now beginning the process of -- we have 19 intercept operators that we'll be calling over the next weeks. The first one is ready to go, and he is still a -- well, if we could go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we do that, I would like to mention something else. I can't see her because she's hiding from my position. I would like to indicate that the Chamber has no objection against the presence of Ms. Djordjevic here in the courtroom. Welcome to this trial, and we wish you good co-operation with everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, naturally there was intercepting going on all sides during the war. The Bosnian Muslim army and the Bosnian Muslim state security forces both were engaged in intercept operations, both wire-tapping and intercepting the radio waves. We do not have any wire-taps in this case, so you will be hearing evidence on radio intercepts that they're getting over the airwaves with radio equipment. And you will be hearing from mostly army intercept people, with a few state Security people, and you'll be hearing the evidence about the size of those two groups. Of the many, many thousands of intercepts in the war that may be relevant, we have chosen about 300 to offer into evidence that are relevant. And a certain number of those are, of course, more relevant, but 300 will be offered. We have offered 27 operators in evidence, 19 that we will bring here as either full witnesses or 92 ter witnesses. The others, we've offered 92 bis. The reason we have chosen to bring some people to court was partly based on the importance of those intercepts, but also largely based on the Rules, in that those intercepts either go to the acts or conducts of the accused, mentioning him, or sometimes his subordinates, or actually important intercepts in the case against him, so we have endeavoured to call these 19 operators so that they could be fully cross-examined because their intercepts have a certain importance to the accused and to the Prosecution, though there is no firm and fast rule why we have chosen some and not others, but it is mostly because of our value judgement that those intercepts were either acts or conduct, which is easy to determine because his name is mentioned or something like that, or other important intercepts. You will find that the intercept operators don't really remember the intercepts, there's just too many, and so we don't generally ask them questions about the substance and the meaning of intercepts because they just don't remember, but the process is what we mostly will talk about. It gets rather repetitive because it's mostly the same process without the topic, but we've done this in the past and we've done it now because we believe, because of the subject matter of the intercepts, the law requires us to do that, because process is very important. And that's fundamentally what I wanted to start you out with so you had the -- just the basic outline of why we're calling so many of these folks, and so you'll be able to distinguish this is a State Security person, this person that we begin with, but it will be mostly army intercept people that you'll be hearing from. And that's all I wanted to say to start out. I have a packet of the intercepts that this particular witness noted down himself. You've got a brief primer when Mr. Kweku Vanderpuye responded to your questions and he explained briefly how the intercepts were listened to and transcribed, and so we have called the intercept operators who were involved in the listening or transcribing of particular intercepts. This witness has 12 such intercepts that we have put in an outline format. There's an outline in the front, and then the intercepts, both English and B/C/S, are in little packets that we have for everyone for your convenience. And I think we have been developing this for each of the intercept operators, if you would so like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, we will have different versions of the original and the translation, and then in that case we should -- you should follow the guide-line of the Chamber related to exhibit numbers, with the number and A, B, C, so that we can identify the version -- the original version and the transcript and the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we understood that, and Ms. Stewart is -- we are in the process of doing that, and I think we're squared away for these first. In addition, this is -- this is not a 92 ter witness, but he does have 12 intercepts. I don't intend -- but we'll see how we do with this. I don't feel, from the Prosecution's perspective or the Court's, that we need to go over each one of them, so I have sort of a shorthand way for him to identify that all of these are his, and I will ask him to talk about one or two of them so you can see -- get an example of it, and that way I may not need to read out all 12 and the numbers associated with them. But we can play it by ear and, of course, see how you feel about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I would like to mention that the Chamber is seized of your submission to change some of the witnesses from 92 bis to 92 ter, and we received yesterday the response by the Defence, and we hope that we will be able to issue a decision as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We are ready to call the first witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If there is nothing further, the witness should be brought in. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since preliminary matters were raised here, and Mr. McCloskey wanted to go straight through to the witness, I would have an administrative matter to raise, by your leave. Thank you. May there be peace in this house, and may God's will be done in these proceedings, and may the outcome be as God wishes. As I was informed by my legal advisor, Mr. Gajic, our submission to have two working days a week was denied and that we should continue by working three days a week up until the summer recess, whereupon the workload would increase. May I give my submissions on the matter? Working more than two days a week will create enormous problems for us, and that's primarily due to the way the transcripts are produced. The transcript of the proceedings is only done in English and French, and that causes a problem for me. When we have a 92 ter witness, there, the normal rules do not apply whereby I should be given all the documentation in both English and B/C/S. In such cases, the transcripts are available only in English and French, whereas for the B/C/S version I can only be given audiotapes. And, of course, you will imagine that I need as many days as I spend in the courtroom here to go through all these audiotapes. Therefore, in keeping with the relevant Articles of the Statute, every accused is entitled to adequate time and resources for the preparation of his defence, and the accused is also entitled to the free-of-charge assistance of an interpreter if he's not able to use the official language of the Tribunal. Therefore, in view of the fact that I need to go through the audio and videotapes to acquaint myself with the earlier testimonies of these witnesses, and since I would require as much time for that as I do for spending in the courtroom, and sometimes even more, I need to be provided with adequate time. Otherwise, I'm only given transcripts. And I need to receive exact references in the transcript that will be used in order for me to ask for their translation into B/C/S. In other words, I need the relevant portions of the transcript translated into B/C/S, and I need them in a timely fashion. The Defence does not have the resources to do this itself. And let me recall that the language assistant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we have listened carefully to your words, but you know the Chamber has ruled on this already. We have taken into account the position of the Prosecution and your submission to this question. We have ruled on that. There is no reason to change our decision at this time. We have taken into account your position, as an accused who is representing himself. This might cause a problem for you in some respects, but, on the other hand, we have to be aware of a very expeditious trial and at the same time a fair trial for you. But we shouldn't continue a discussion about that because we have ruled on that, and you are aware of our decision, and we should use the court time for evidence, hearing the witness. Do you have any other matter, despite this --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm not talking about your decision at all. I'm talking about my need to have transcripts, and that may be the subject of your next decision to allocate an interpreter to me and resources to pay that interpreter or to have transcripts given to me in the Serbian language. I'm not talking about the decision you have already made, or maybe I did not make myself clear. But if Article 21 of the Statute applies to me as well in its point 4, stipulating that I should have adequate time and resources to prepare, then provisions should be made for that. And I'm not talking about the decision you have already made. I'm talking about something that needs to be done. And I suggest that you allocate to me an interpreter and adequate resources and transcripts in the language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I stop you here. I think if there is any argument, any need for that, you should do that in writing and submit that to the Chamber in writing. I think it's a more appropriate way to deal with your problem you have raised here. I hope that is the best way to deal with this problem. If there are no other matters --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will submit that to you. But do you really need it in writing that I need transcripts and that I need to refer to transcripts as an exhibit? It is up to you to decide how these transcripts will be made available to me. If we have trials three or four days a week, I have no time for that. I have no time to listen to an interpreter translating to me what's written in the transcripts or to study that. Of course, if you need a written submission, I will make it, but we've been here for three years, and I still haven't got the transcripts of the pre-trial conferences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we have now your position on the record. The Chamber will consider your submission in due course, and now we should stop the discussion about this topic here in the courtroom. We want to use the court time for evidence. But we will consider your position. The witness should be --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, but I have not finished with the problems that I need to notify you of. I have more problems, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, in this case it would be more appropriate if you could do that in writing so that we have all your arguments in front of us and the Prosecution could respond to that. I think if this is a real serious problem, you should raise it in writing in order to avoid to waste court time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already told you of another of my problem, that I'm being woken up every 10 or 20 minutes, which is many times a night. I haven't seen it in the practice of any kind of medicine, that waking a person up can be beneficial, medically. And I've been here for three years, and this has been going on. I've already made a written submission of that. I don't know how I can stand trial if I'm allowed no rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are aware of the fact that the Chamber has asked the Registry to provide us with a new status of your health situation. And we will receive a report by the medical doctor of the UNDU and an independent medical doctor, and I think then at that time we should come back to this problem again. You see, the Chamber always considers your concerns to every respect and what you are raising, but I think you should stop this discussion. And when you say you need more time to explain something, please do it in writing. It's better for finding a proper decision.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, until now 20 submissions have been written about the problem of the satanic methods used against me in the Detention Unit and the fact that I'm being woken up every now and then, and the Trial Chamber has already ruled that it is all right. Now you need more time for consideration. By the time you decide to deal with it, half of the trial will be over. I don't see what more you need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is not a correct statement. You will be aware of the fact that the Pre-Trial Chamber was dealing with this problem. Since the trial has started, this problem was not notified to the Chamber. It was now notified. You mentioned this problem in your response dealing with the scheduling order of the Chamber, and this is the reason - you know that - why we asked the Registry to provide us with a new medical report of the relevant medical doctors. I think we should stop the discussion here. It is not very sufficient to go on, on this topic, before we receive the medical report, and then we will be able to deal with this. The witness should be brought in now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. You mind that I'm talking for five minutes. Can you imagine how much I mind that this issue is being considered for three years now by the Pre-Trial Chamber or the Trial Chamber. It's about my sleep, my rest, my state of health. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand your position, Mr. Tolimir. We are aware of that. And it is raised for the first time with this Trial Chamber, and we are taking the necessary steps to inquire into the situation. You are aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. We apologise for the late start of your evidence because of several procedural matters. They have to be discussed here in the courtroom. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think you are aware of the fact that the protective measures are still in place for you. Mr. McCloskey has some questions for you, and I would like to remind the parties to switch off the microphones during the answers of the witness. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning. First, could we pull up on the screen what we call the pseudonym sheet, which is 65 ter 6278. And we need to do this in open session, but this should not, of course, be broadcast. And hopefully you will see something on the sheet that you will recognise. And, sir, do you see your name on this sheet?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could offer that into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go into private --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P237, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Private session, please, for personal details. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, can you, first of all, tell us where you were born and when?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I was born on the 2nd of June, 1962, in Brnjik, Celic municipality. Before the war, it was Lupar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that in -- was that in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you are a Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for us your education as you grow up; where you went to school, what kind of schooling you took?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Chronologically, you mean? I finished higher -- the High School of Electrical Engineering in 1982. Then I went to serve my regular military service. And then I found employment in the State Security Service. In 1991, I believe, I finished my university studies, becoming a teacher of engineering. That was schooling on the job. And some years ago, I continued my education and became a professor of engineering. I still work for the same service, which was renamed in the meantime. It was first the State Security Service, then it was the Agency for Investigations and Documentation, and then it became FOS, and now it's called OSA, which is the Intelligence Agency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what year did you do your regular JNA military service?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: In the course of my regular JNA military service, I was -- I was an operator on anti-tank guided missiles. But just after I finished primary school, I became a Ham radio operator and joined a club. And until 10 years ago, I was very active in one of the radio clubs in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is a Ham radio club? What is this? It's, I think, otherwise known as amateur radio club. What is that about, just briefly, so we understand.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: All right. Radio amateurism is a worldwide movement wherein people use radio stations and communicate on ultra-short radio airwaves according to regulations that are accepted in the field, and they understand each other very well. They keep up friendships and maintain a system of radio communications that was of great assistance in cases of natural disasters throughout the world, including in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And through these clubs, through this movement, during the war, for instance, Ham radio operators helped establish connections between people and the outside world.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do these Ham radio clubs have, generally throughout the world, a governmental connection, or is it civilian in nature?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Those are civilian associations. They have nothing to do with politics or with the state. The only point of contact with the state is that if some assistance is needed in the activities of the clubs, like regional or state or international competitions, we would ask for financial aid from the state. But those were very small amounts, and mainly it was financed from the pocket of the members. The state would sometimes provide premises for our activities, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can go into open. That could have been in open, but he got me into Ham radios before I caught us. So we can go back into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Open.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, sir, when the war broke --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, when the war broke out in Bosnia in the spring of 1992, what job did you hold?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: When the war broke out, I was working with the State Security Service in communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And at some point did you become the chief of a small unit to intercept radio communications near the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes. That clearly became a necessary activity towards the end of 1994. There was a real need for such a unit, because we were able to engage only a limited number of staff on that job to obtain the information necessary to the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And could we go into private session just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've described that there was an army unit there. Can you describe what kind of terrain feature this northern site is?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: It's a rather well-known elevation in the army, at least because it's very favourable for this purpose. And as far as I know, the army had its own listening equipment there. And in 1992, I believe this location was taken up by the 2nd Corps of the BH Army, or, rather, they detached a section. What is it called? It was one anti-electronic security company of the 2nd Corps. I don't know how many men there were in that company, but they had their own security people and operators who were doing the listening and intercepting. It was a fully-equipped installation with all the infrastructure, and we realised it was a good location with very amenable conditions for our own work with our own staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you very briefly describe what was it about this location that made it a good location to intercept?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, it was located in the north, at a good altitude that offered a range of possibilities. At least I had the information that according to previous analysis, it was found to be a very good location for intercepting. Its size and altitude and location made it very good for that purpose. Perhaps there were better locations, but, as I said, we had to use the infrastructure of the army or some other agency in order to be able to do our work with the limited number of personnel we had. It was open towards the north and the east, and it even had the possibility, by the reflection of airwaves against mountains, of giving us some signals that were important to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall roughly what the elevation above sea level was of this elevation?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Around 800, 815 metres, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in 1995, can you describe the size of your unit and what your position was regarding that unit as it worked up at the northern site?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes. Back in 1992, I was with a unit that was involved in similar work, and this unit grew out of that previous one. So in 1994 I was appointed chief of that section, and in 1995 we came to that location, we installed equipment that had been already prepared. And throughout our work, this section had only four men. Two men worked per shift, and they had a clearly-identified assignment to collect as much information as two men could get. In addition, I was also in charge of another section at the base, and because the connection between these two units were very close, I served them both. And in 1995, because of the events that occurred, I was at the location myself very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You've described the four-people unit that does intercepting. And what is this other unit that you were also part of that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: It was a communications and crypto-protection squad. It is very similar work that it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's start in a description of the process with the equipment. What is the -- what is the first thing you need to actually intercept radio waves?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: The work that we did was not represented in my service. It was something new. And because that was so, we had to consult experts who were in the 2nd Corps PBA unit at the time. They were familiar with the equipment that the VRS had and which it had inherited from the JNA. They knew what communications equipment it was, what were the waves and the frequencies, and they had already adapted a new technique and a new set of equipment that they could use in order to intercept this kind of military equipment used by the other side. So with their assistance, we also adapted several radio sets, which we then brought to this location. We also had professional-type antenna, the so-called Top antenna, which is directional. So with these several machines that we had for recording communication, and with two men, we went up to the said location. We also had a computer at the beginning in which we would type the information that we obtained. Initially, we also could not send the information to our base. We did not have the technical ability for that, but we managed to enable that later on. At the beginning, we would use the PEB communications system of the 2nd Corps to transmit the information, and they would use floppy discs and then submit them to my service. So in order to monitor and intercept radio waves, we had monitors, we had an antenna and an amplifier, an antenna input connector, because each frequency had 24 channels in the radio relay systems. We also had UHERs, that is to say, reel-to-reel tape recorders that we used to record conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just have you go through that piece by piece very briefly. You mention that you had antennas. Can you describe where those antennas were and who built those antennas?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: We received the first antenna. It was issued to me I don't remember where, but my service had one antenna of the kind, so it was given to me for use. It was the so-called Top antenna. It was part of the communications equipment of the former JNA, and it was painted olive-drab. We also used several other directional antennae for the ultra-short range of frequencies. The antennae were then taken from a radio club in Tuzla, in addition to a set of other equipment, such as cables and connectors, that we used in order to set all this up. We also had a so-called stick antenna with which we should also listen to certain frequencies. There were several spectrums that we could monitor from the ultra-short, two-metre-range radio telephones. They were open and not coded at the time, so one could listen to them directly. Also, RRU 100 and RRU 800 were the radio relay frequencies that we could listen to. After that, in 1995, when there was a need for better-quality antennae, as there were some signals that we could only get a glimpse of, we could not really hear them well, then we received a parabolic antenna. I cannot remember exactly, but it was about two metres in diametre, and we set it up on a street light pole that was maybe eight metres tall at that time. We attached it with steel ropes because it was at the top of the mountain, so it had to withstand the strong winds that were blowing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were all these mounted at the top of the mountain at the site?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm talking about the same location, and all the antennae were placed at this location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So after the antenna -- basically, tell us, very simply, what does the antenna do?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: The antenna is a piece of equipment which receives electronic waves and brings them to a radio receiver, so that's the simplest way to put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you've mentioned that you had radio sets, and you mentioned that you amplified the waves, and now you've said the waves come to the radio receiver. And how -- what does the operator do? What equipment does the operator that's at the site have in front of him? Can you describe that process for us.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes. We had several devices for listening and for monitoring a range of frequencies, as I mentioned earlier. Over time, by listening, we would single out what may be interesting, and the operator who is sitting there at his work-place already had certain ranges of frequencies or channels that he was supposed to monitor, because we had already decided on these ranges of frequencies earlier. So he would scan these channels or ranges of frequencies, and at the moment when he would listen and hear a conversation, then we would stop the device and then turn on the recording device. That's one possibility. Another one is once we had determined certain priorities, we would have a device that would only monitor one particular channel, so we would wait for someone to pick up the telephone receiver and the device would begin to record at the very same instant. Once a conversation had been recorded, as there were two men working there, one of them or both would continue listening, but one would begin to produce a transcript of the conversation. So after it was transcribed on paper, he would sit down in front of a computer and he would type it up and turn it into an electronic form, into a file, that would be sent to the seat of our service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that the radio waves come in, the different channels are scanned. When the operator hears a conversation, he may, you said, depress something and begin to record that conversation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This is a device, the UHER reel-to-reel tape-recorder, with big tapes, which also has the possibility of pause. If there is a conversation, there is a pause button, so you just press the pause button and the device begins to record. It's a reel-to-reel tape-recorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you used this -- called UHER, U-H-E-R, UHER tape -- just a regular reel-to-reel tape-recorder that used to be used quite a bit more than it is used now?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And at what point in this process did the other operator start transcribing the conversation that had been heard and then started to be recorded?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to think back to the time. As I said, very often I was present at the site myself, and depending on the urgency of the information, it might happen that we would have two consecutive conversations, and so the time of recording and sending the conversation to the base could be a bit late. But if there was something that we called very urgent at the time, then we would separate this conversation from the others, and it would immediately be transcribed and sent to the base. It also sometimes happened that if a conversation was very interesting or if it was carried out in another language, because we didn't have interpreters with us, then we would have to bring these recordings on tape to the seat of our service. And then if the conversation was, for example, in English, it would be translated. And if it was very urgent, then it would be re-recorded into another medium and then brought to a higher level, that is to say, to our superiors in the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the typical process by which one operator would take this UHER machine, as you've described it, and listen to a taped conversation and transcribe it? How did that work? First of all, where did that happen? Did it happen right there, where the other person was listening, or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Everything was taking place in one-and-the-same room, absolutely everything. We had a big desk on which one person would listen, and there was a separate place for transcription. So once we recorded something, when it was on tape, recorded by the UHER device, then the other operator would take that, he would sit down, put it in his own UHER for transcription, and he would transcribe the conversation. Once they were transcribed, they would also include the time when it was intercepted, then also the channel, the frequency, and possibly the persons who were the participants in the conversation. And then he would begin to transcribe the conversation on the reel-to-reel tape-recorder which he had in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did the UHER reel-to-reel tape-recorder have the ability to have earphones?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, we had earphones on all devices that we used; however, depending on the need. Whenever we were transcribing, one had to put on the earphones, but if during the transcribing process the other operator was listening, then he would also put on the earphones so that he would not cause any trouble for the one who was transcribing the conversation. Once transcribed, the conversation would be typed out into the computer, and it would be placed in the then improvised log-book, where we would have the ordinal number for the transcribed information, then also the time when it was sent, the number assigned by the computer during the encoding before it was sent to our central. It had to be crypto-protected because it was sent by the wireless method and later on also through telephone wires. But, in any case, the rules were such that every file had to be crypto-protected. So in the log-book there would also be the number assigned by the computer to the crypto-protected file, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how simple or difficult was it to transcribe these intercepted conversations? How hard was that process, normally? How long would it take a typical -- an operator to transcribe something like that?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: It all depended. It depended on the quality of the signal, on the quality of audibility. Sometimes it happened that the signal was exceptionally good, and then transcription was very easy and very quick. However, there were also instances when the signal was of poor quality, and, therefore, in our transcripts, in places when we couldn't hear something well, you will see dots. That means that we could not hear the participants in the conversation and did not transcribe anything. If we didn't hear the name of the participant, then we would put an X or a Y to denote these people. And how long did it last? Well, that depended on the length of the conversation and the audibility. However, we always tried to transcribe a conversation as quickly as possible and then send it to our seat. Sometimes we could make a selection of the information that we received, and then we could say, Well, for these conversations we can wait until the afternoon, when we may have more time, or until any moment when we have more free time. And then we would select some as priority conversations because they were urgent. That's how we would do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would the transcriber ever listen to the tape more than once in his attempt to transcribe it?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes. Once again, it depended on the quality. It happened often that there were three of us. We would all take earphones and listen to something so that we would be certain about what we were transcribing, because it was in no one's interest that the information that might be incorrect would eventually be used. That would be a scandal for us, in the first place. So very often all three of us would listen to something, and if we were not certain, we would just put three dots, because we would then denote that we couldn't really hear that part of the conversation. Later on, when this was listened to at the seat, I would sometimes hear that the operator who was working on a conversation might hear something, but nothing changed in the transcription. In terms of operative use, they might use the information if they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, on that topic, can you describe how important an object it was for you, if at all, to make this accurate?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: That was of utmost importance, because this was information that was so significant that it simply couldn't be allowed to happen that we would transcribe something that we didn't hear. That was in nobody's interest, and particularly at the time when the information was used on an hour-to-hour basis. Can you just imagine what would happen if we would transmit false information? Nobody needed that. That was operative information to be used during the day for all kinds of needs. I don't really know what all the needs could have been, because we were only in charge of the work that I described, but I know that the rule was to mark with dots something that we could not hear or to denote the participants in a conversation with an X or a Y. Sometimes it happened that a man would introduce himself, but we didn't know who that was. In such cases, we would say, One so-and-so, or, A certain so-and-so, because we were not certain if this was really that particular person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you ever able to identify anybody in these conversations by recognising their voice?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Certainly. There were public figures, military or political ones, whose voice would be recognised by any citizen, not just us. There were also those that we identified because they introduced themselves. They would say, So-and-so is speaking. Can I please speak with so-and-so? So we always used that as well. There were also instances, I just remember now, when there would be a new person who introduced himself by first and last name. Then we would keep the recording so that if there was the same person speaking later on in another conversation, we would compare the voice to make sure if it was really that person or not. It was really a very serious and responsible approach that we used, and of course not with the consequences that we are seeing now in mind. We never thought that that would be used for needs such as the current ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you'd mentioned that the three of you would all listen. Were you saying that you would all listen -- that sometimes all three of you would listen to the same conversation, or were you talking about all three of you listening to separate conversations when doing the transcribing process?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: No, no. When the operator is transcribing a conversation and something is hard to understand, he would ask us, Please tell me, what do you hear? It depends on a certain person, what one hears or not. So perhaps we might reach an agreement, and we would say, Yes, that's what he says. If we were not certain, we would place the dots. So it was the only situation in which we would not listen on three separate channels, because we would try to help and create a real picture of what was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When the transcriber is listening to the UHER, what is he -- what is he doing? Is he writing, or typing, or how is he actually transcribing what he's hearing, and what's he transcribing it onto?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Once the tape with the recording is in place in the UHER, the operator plays it. Then he listens to one part of it. Then he presses the pause button, and then he writes that section on paper. Then again he presses the pause button. Then he plays it back, if he needs to, so that he would connect everything with the previous part of the conversation, and then he writes again and writes again, and this is what he does. And in the end, he plays once again the entire conversation, he has the paper in front of him, and then he can check if everything is correct or not. So that was how a conversation would be transcribed. The operator has in front of him the UHER device and the tape, which he can play back to the previous section of the conversation. He notes everything on paper, and then he types it out into the computer from the paper. And then every day we would destroy these papers because that was the rule. Sometimes we would do it more frequently if we had a number collected already. I mean the papers that we used to write in hand the transcript of the conversation that was intercepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So you destroy the paper used to transcribe. What about the tapes, themselves, that you've now taped a conversation that you've heard? What was done with those tapes?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I have to admit we had a very limited number of tapes. We did not have a sufficient number of tapes, so we used the available tapes for recordings. Once the conversations were transcribed, we would bring all the papers together, and we would burn them, because we already had it in electronic form then. If we estimated that certain conversations were exceptionally interesting and that they needed special attention, then we would re-record them onto a big tape and we would mark on the UHER that the conversation between X and Y was recorded from a certain number, 123 to 360 on the tape counter, an exceptionally interesting conversation between X and Y. So we would re-record such conversations to such tapes. These tapes we would bring to the seat, and we would submit them to those who would then use the information that we received at our location in any way in which that was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have many such transcripts of intercepted conversations and some actual tapes that you had saved been provided to the ICTY for these -- for this Tribunal's use?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I know that some had been provided. When the request arrived from the ICTY, somebody gave me a call and asked me to re-record certain recordings to a different medium so that they might be forwarded, so I know that some were provided. But other than that, I'm not aware of it, since it wasn't part of my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've mentioned briefly that the transcribed conversation got typed into a computer, encrypted, and then sent, via computer secure means, somewhere. Where did the computer send this material?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: The material, that's to say the file in the electronic form, would be sent to the communications centre of my service. It would be recorded in the log-book that they used there, in other words filed, and sent to the head of service that was in charge of this sort of work. The files would be sent through communications equipment, and for a while these were two radio sets that were directed one toward the other, with the help of antenna, and they used ultra-short waves. This was the way in which these files were transmitted. Later on, we had the telephone line, which was a more secure way of transmitting information. There were also special cases when, and I believe I've already mentioned this, files would be taken personally since that location wasn't that far removed. These were special events involving specific information. When speed was required, then these files would be taken by individuals, who would use their cars to reach the head office, the seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Very well. We must have the first break now. The Court Officer will assist you during the break, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, what I was getting at is, at some point after you transmit these intercepts, do they go for analysis somewhere?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: After they reach the communications centre in an encrypted form, the operators at the operations centre would decipher the conversation, print it out, and take it to the head of the relevant organisational unit, who would, in turn, pass them on to operatives or otherwise employees of the service who were charged with doing precisely that sort of work. In other words, they would be using the information thus received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you share any of your intercepts that you received with the army that you were working with up there?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Let me just briefly go back to one point. Every intercept would be signed by the individual who taped the intercept and who transcribed it. This is something that I omitted to say earlier on. Once the intercept has been transcribed, it would be signed. You saw that there was a combination of numbers and letters which denoted individuals. The first number, combined with -- the first, that's to say, letter combined with numbers would denote the individual who taped the conversation, then you would have a dash and a different combination of letter and numbers denoting another operator, the one who transcribed the conversation. Now, what was your conversation again? My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we will get to a couple of examples so you can point out the numbers and what they mean, so that can be easily understood. And the translation I got is that the operator actually signed an intercept, and the way it's translated to me, as if somebody did a handwritten signature. What do you mean when an intercept operator signed these intercepts? Because you're talking about just destroying the transcription version and then typing in, in an electronic version, so what do you precisely mean when you say "signed"?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: What I meant to say was that every transcription, once it was completed and in an electronic form, at the bottom of it there had to be written who the recording and who the transcribing operator was. If there was only one such combination of codes, it would mean that the same operator recorded and transcribed the intercept, although in the majority of cases we would have one recording operator and another transcribing operator. And by having this information on the intercept, you would know that there were two operators who did the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so my original question was: Did you share any of your intercepts with the army, and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: At a certain stage, and I can't recall exactly the time-period this was, we made an arrangement. In view of the assessed needs and the use of the information we came by at these sites, we made an arrangement with the army, that's to say, representatives of the 2nd Corps, the PEB of the 2nd Corps, that whatever information we come by, we should convey to them, and they should do likewise. The practical reason behind this was to ensure proper and full use of information at different levels, though my assumption is that the information converged anyhow from both these entities, and this would ultimately mean that both entities would have the same set of information. We thought it was justified, and that's how we did the work for a certain period of time. I can also explain it to you in the following manner: Our primary objective was to monitor civilian structures, yet there were cases where we would intercept conversations that were of a military nature, and it would be a pity if we did not convey this sort of information to the military structures in addition to our own service. So that was the practicality of the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've partly answered my next question, and that was: Did you have a -- what was your focus, as opposed to your knowledge of what the military focus was, as you were out there listening over the airwaves? Was it the same or different?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: It was different. I explained that oftentimes quite the opposite would happen. Our goal was to collect information from civilian structures present in an area of interest to us. The objective was also to monitor and obtain information about the civilian authorities of the opposite side. As you will know, oftentimes the two overlap, and the intercepts testify to the fact that this, indeed, happened. Whenever we intercepted this sort of information, we felt the need to convey it to the army in order that the army may be able to adequately respond and in order that the information may be put to full use by the army. Specifically, we had information about the movements of troops and their intentions, et cetera. There were cases where specific routes or links that we monitored, which were set aside for specific individuals, did not result in any specific information because these individuals would not engage in conversation. In such cases, we would turn to different channels that we would listen to, and this would sometimes overlap with what the army was doing, and they would be able to come by the same information that we did. I did not necessarily check whether this was the case or whether they did, indeed, receive the same information as we did, but the possibility was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to now go -- well, first of all, let me ask you, as you first -- you've testified in several cases, and when you were first, many years ago, coming to The Hague and beginning your testifying, did you or your colleagues remember much about the actual substance of any of these intercepts, what they said, what they meant?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, we were able to -- we were able to recall a great deal of these intercepts. Some of them were very important and remained etched in our memory, but in retrospect, after a number of years where I was occupied on a different sort of work, I can conclude that the memories have faded and the years have left their mark. Now, when I look at some of these intercepts, some of them do bring back memories, and vivid ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll go over a few of those intercepts to help explain what you have been talking about. And if we could start with 65 ter 2923, and this is number 3 in the little booklet. And I would like us to try to focus, if we could, Mr. President, on the B/C/S version because, as you'll see, it's a little different than the English translation, and there's a specific reason for that which we will get to. All right. If we could just -- that looks good. So looking at this intercept, the B/C/S typed version, we see the beginning says -- we need the top part. You had it just right. Okay, that's fine. First of all, before I get into the detail of what "CSB" and that means, can you tell us what this is? Where does this fit into the process of intercepts that you've described? We see here, actually, multiple intercepts with different "Broj"s, with different numbers. The first one we see, 556 and then 557. So what is this list that we see of -- the total, I think, is three intercepts, 556, 557, and 558. What is this sheet of paper we're looking at? Where does it fit into what you've been testifying about?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: This is a report, and I believe that it can be found in one of the encrypted files that we talked about. At any rate, what this means is that several intercepts were recorded on one reel, on one tape, and they had to be transcribed. As soon as the operator had time available to start transcribing the recordings, he transcribed two, three, or more intercepts, depending on how many had been recorded in the meantime. Sometimes there would only be one intercept. It depended. We can see here that these conversations were short. It all depended on the situation and on how much time the transcribing operator had. In this particular instance, several intercepts were incorporated into one report. We were under the obligation to record every particular intercept under a different number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, we see the English on the other side. It's only a translation of intercept 557, which is the only intercept that we're offering from this individual report. We have not put a date above it, because that would not have been an appropriate translation, because you can see that the date is above the main report. So in order to get the date of the English, you need to go to the B/C/S. You see where it is in the overall report. You go to the top of the page, and you'll see the date. So that's why the English translation is only the intercept we are looking at, but to understand how it fits in, as he's just testified about it. So I hope that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To clarify the situation, there's only one original version in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. As you will recall, the transcripted versions that the witness talked about, as the State Security -- after they typed it into the computer, they destroyed their handwritten versions. The next witness you'll hear from the army, and that's where it gets more complicated, because we have those handwritten transcripted versions, and that's where this complication arrives. This is less complicated for our purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 2923 will be Exhibit P239.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So let's focus on the top of the page. It says "CSB - SDB Tuzla." Can you tell us what those initials mean?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes. "CSB" stands for the Security Services Centre. Within the Security Services Centre, there existed the Public Security Sector and State Security Sector. So within this particular CSB, Security Services Centre, we were the state -- within the Security Centre, we were the State Security Service, if that's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that means the SDB is the State Security Service?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then the next line we see "Dana" or "Date," and then "12 July 1995, and a "G." What does that date have to do with these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: This document was produced on this date, and then what follows next is a link between the date and what follows next, because it is stated that on the said date, whilst monitoring the radio relay route, et cetera, the following conversation was captured, and, of course, as a follow-up that's how this document came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we did not translate that, so can you please read that statement for us slowly so we can see what it is, that one that begins with "Navedenog"?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes. On the said date, whilst monitoring the RR radio relay route, quote/unquote, "Zvornik - Vlasenica," on the frequency of 785.000 megahertz, at 0822 hours, on channel 11, we have registered a conversation between one Miro, who would be hereinafter referred to as "M," and an unknown, unidentified male, who would be referred to in the text as "X."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony you've mentioned many kinds of equipment you were able to -- or many kinds of radio waves you were able to intercept. One of those things you mentioned was radio relay waves, and since that is most of the intercepts you will be talking about, can you describe to us briefly, when you're intercepting radio relay waves, what is this radio relay, and especially as opposed to people talking on what we know as a hand-held walkie-talkie in the woods to each other?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Let me first note that I did not have specialised training in this field when I first took up this work. All the technical knowledge and the knowledge concerning the equipment used by the other side was something that I received from the PEB of -- that's to say the Counter-Electronic Protection of the 2nd Corps, and it was in this way that I learned which frequency ranges were used by the other side and what sort of equipment the military on the other side had. I know that this specific frequency was connected to the radio sets RRU 800. This was a telephone communication taking place between interlocutors who could have a complete network along these routes without using lines or wires. Through certain switch boards, town telephone lines could be connected to them as well. What mattered to us was to come by information as to what the frequency range used by the other side was in order for us to be able to listen in. As far as I remember now, and I can't state this with certainty, this frequency range was between 600-and-something megahertz up to 900-odd megahertz. With the help of specialists from the PEB of the 2nd Corps, and with the help of digital equipment that was available and which could define the range, we did the scanning. And on the basis of this, we were able to select the frequency that we would listen in to, and we could proceed intercepting conversations on these frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I don't want to take you into that very complicated area. There will be -- the army experts will talk about it. But just very simply, what is a radio relay?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't have interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A radio relay route is, to put it simply, a route where we have a device and an antenna on one end and a device and an antenna on the other end; that is to say, the same equipment on both ends of the route. And when a person picks up a telephone receiver on one end, through these devices and this antenna they can emit a signal to the other end, to be captured by the other device and antenna. Since we are talking about radio waves, normally the rule is that these signals should be as distant from the other side as possible so as to prevent the monitoring and listening and interception. However, there are also other rules in emitting waves which tell us that waves reflect from mountains, obstacles, and structures, and that makes communication porous and susceptible to interception.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to this intercept and the B/C/S one. And if we could scroll down towards the bottom, through the various intercepts. And I think we have to go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you just tell us, "Tona Benzina," is that part of the intercept? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: That's part of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then can you tell us what "JN160/JD065" is, those letters and numbers?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: This is what I mentioned earlier. These are designations of the names of the operators who did this at the time. I said this first number, JN160, is the operator who recorded the conversations, and this other initial and number is the person who transcribed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is one of those numbers your number?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I want to ask you about one more intercept, and that is 65 ter 2932. And if we could get both of them up on the screen. If we can blow the B/C/S up, we see that same heading, the date of 12 July. We see two intercepts here, and again we see your number down at the bottom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I am interested in intercept number 570, which is what we have the English. And let me just read it out. It says: "On the above-mentioned day, intercepting the Zvornik-Vlasenica radio-relay route frequency 785.000, channel 5, we registered at 1250 hours a conversation between General Mladic, (M), and an unidentified male person, (X). The conversation proceeded as follows: "X: Go ahead, General. "M" for Mladic: "Have these buses and trucks left? "X: They have. "M: When? "X: 10 minutes ago. "M: Good, excellent. Continue to monitor the situation. Don't let small groups of them sneak in. They've all capitulated and surrendered, and we'll evacuate them all - those who want to and those who don't want to. "X: I understand, General. "M: Don't issue any statements and don't interrupt them over the," question mark, "radio." That's our -- I'm sorry, the double slash is the translation people, Your Honours: "We'll open a corridor towards Kladanj. "X: .... "M: Indeed, let it pass there. Take a patrol of ours to wait on the road and remove the mines and obstacles ... leave the territory. "X: Yes, General." Now, in the heading of this intercept, it says that this is a conversation with General Mladic. In the substance of the intercept, we don't hear General Mladic introduce himself or anyone refer to him as General Mladic. And, as you said, that was one way that people could be identified. So how, if you know, can this intercept conclude in its heading that General Mladic is, in fact, the "M" in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: There are several ways here. One of the ways is that before this conversation was intercepted, we had heard Mladic loads of times, we played back and transcribed his conversations, we watched him on television, and since we are talking here about two people who are doing this job and this job only, they simply can't be mistaken. Another way is that at the beginning of the conversation, the operator heard a reference to General Mladic, but did not have time to switch in and start the recording at that moment. By the time recording started, that part of the conversation was already gone, and he then transcribed only the recorded part, indicating that it was a conversation involving General Mladic. We were quite certain, when Mladic was concerned and many other people were monitored, that this was, indeed, the person in question because the voice was quite recognisable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And near the end of the conversation, we see, after "X," a series of dots. Can you describe to us what that means, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes. I think I've already said a few words about this. These are the passages when the other side was not very well heard. It's about a technical problem. With these relay communications on RRU 800, there are two frequencies on which a conversation develops. The speaking of one person is on one frequency. The other person speaks on another frequency. Now, with the headphones we are using, when playing back one, we also hear the other. Later on, we managed to locate the other frequency of the other speaker, so we managed to get better-quality intercepts involving both. In such passages, when we were not quite certain what the person on the other end was saying, we put a number of dots.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If the speaker's on one frequency and the other speaker is on another, how is it that an operator, having tapped into one frequency, can hear two at the same time?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that when audibility is good, when we have a good signal on one frequency, then it happens that we are able to hear the other end as well through a micro-telephone combination. We hear the other person in a more muffled way, less distinctly than the person we are monitoring, but we still hear them. Later on, we identify the other frequency as well so we get both ends of the conversation, but very often we are able to hear the other speaker as well. It happens sometimes that people blurt out things very fast and we can't be sure what they actually said, and we put dots, or perhaps a person uses a word or a term unfamiliar to us, and then we do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This particular intercept with Mladic, have you had any independent recollection of this intercept over the years?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: There were many, many conversations relating to the organisation of transports. There were many bus transports to be organised, including Holijas [phoen] from Serbia. I can't say that I remember this specific one, but I remember that there were many conversations similar to this. I can't remember this particular one, but, generally speaking, I remember conversations regarding evacuations, organising vehicles and fuel for buses and trucks, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go to 65 ter 6287 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Witness, you will recognise a scanned version of a document, I believe, and it will come up in a minute. That's not the -- I'm sorry, that's not the document I'm looking for. Yes, 65 ter 1680. I apologise. Could we just blow this up. I don't need anything in particular about this. I would just like a general explanation of what this is. Can you tell us what this is, Witness?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes. This is a copy of one page from the log-book into which we entered the information we had forwarded to the communications centre of the State Security Service in Tuzla. It is divided into a number of columns, and on this sheet we see the following, if you want me to explain what is in which column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, if you can, briefly, especially as they relate to the intercepts we just saw, but just generally.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: The first column is the sequential number. The second column is the number of the report. Column 3 is the file created in the computer. Column 4 is the time when the operator forwarded this information to the communications centre. And then the same range of columns repeats itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And does this have anything to do with you? Whose notes are these?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, it does relate to me. These are entries that I started. I defined the format. Some of the entries may have been made by me, but perhaps not. I would have to refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was that the log-book you referred to earlier in your testimony, when you were describing the process?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, that's the log-book. It was a black agenda book that we used as a log-book. And there is other content from that period in the log-book which does not concern this type of information and the forwarding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would offer this exhibit into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now could we go to the -- when we get a number --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1680 is now Exhibit P240.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And, Mr. McCloskey, what about the previous document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart asked me the same question. I will have 12 intercepts which I have -- I was going to try to offer in a format in a minute or two, as opposed to calling out each individual one of them, but I'm just trying to meet what you might want to do in this situation. I can, of course, offer them individually as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's just offer the previous one into evidence right now, and I'll show -- and that's 2932, and then we'll get to these others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P241.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now could we have Exhibit 6287.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you recognise your initials or your handwriting on this document?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see that there are references to 12 intercepts. Did you have a chance to look at the print-outs of all of those 12 intercepts and confirm that you were involved either in the transcription or the recording of all 12 of them?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
