utterances.text: Yes, I reviewed all of them. I compared to this list and confirmed it was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the note-book that we saw the five pages from previously, have we -- and you requested that the original come up in the next -- hopefully the next few days so that we have access to the original note-book.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I expect that we will receive that note-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we look at each of these intercepts, and can we find their numbers in the note-book?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P242.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, that finishes my direct, but that does leave 11 other intercepts that I would like to offer into evidence. I can go over them individually, or they are all on that last exhibit by our numbers. However you would like to do it. I also have -- we, of course, have what Ms. Stewart typed out that has all the exhibits, the map, the five pages out of his note-book, and the 12 intercepts and the pseudonym sheet all on one thing, so I'm at your service to do however you would like to do it. I can read them all out and get all numbers for them right now, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I think the most sufficient way is that you just give the number of the 65 ter document, and the Registrar will give an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. The first one is 2909.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P243.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then 2920.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P244.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The next one is already in. Then 2930.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P245.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The next one is already in. Then 2968.

utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P246.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then 2971.

utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P247.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P248.

utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P249.

utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P250.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P251.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P252.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I offer all of those exhibits. Those have been identified by him as ones that he took part in and that are part of our larger group that we will be offering as we go along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They are received and have an exhibit number. That concludes your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe so, yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Tolimir, do you have questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would like to welcome and greet this witness and everyone in the courtroom, and I wish that his testimony be completed in keeping with God's will, as everything in this trial. Witness, I will be careful not to mention your name. But if you notice that I have said anything identifying, you can alert us immediately, because the broadcasting of your testimony -- the broadcasting of these intercepts is not allowed. Will you please watch the transcript, and when you see that the typing has finished, then start your answer so we don't overlap. I will now start the questioning. A moment ago during examination-in-chief, you told Mr. McCloskey that you were a radio amateur in 1994 and 1995. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I was a radio amateur from - let me think - 1977, and I still am today.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What kind of certificate did you have at that time?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: B category.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you explain what that means, a B-category certificate?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: You're obviously familiar with these things, and you know that there is A, B, C, and D categories in radio amateur activity, and they reflect the speed of receipt and writing down of signals, as well as familiarity with the rules of radio traffic and the radio amateur movement. You have to pass exams to get a different -- a higher class, and I had a B category.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What is your current category?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I have the B category, but I've said that for a while now. I haven't had the time to work as a radio amateur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm grateful that you gave some guidance to the witness to pause before starting the answer, but you should pause as well. It's a big problem for the interpreters. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you said during the examination-in-chief that it was only 1994 when you set up an intercept unit. Did I understand that correctly or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, in 1994 it was officially set up, this group or unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, by whose decision was the group formed? Was it your personal decision or a decision of one of your superiors? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: You know very well that such decisions cannot be made by any leader at a lower level. It was decided at the highest level of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us why, during the remaining part of the war, until 1994, such an intercept group was not set up? Why was it only set up in late 1994 and early 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I couldn't give you an answer to that question because that would be discussion on a topic which has to do with certain duties and decisions, which I do not think are the reason why I am here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, what was the month in the year 1994 when the intercept group was set up? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: As far as I remember, our first duty which was specific was given to us in December 1994. That means that we had the resources, the people were assigned, and we had premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As it was in December 1994, and that was towards the end of the war, can you tell me who was giving you instructions for your work and for setting up the intercept group? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: That was not the end of the war. It was December 1994, which means that the war lasted for another year. And as for instructions, I rather wouldn't talk about that unless the Trial Chamber decides that I have to. After all, I think I have said a lot about the entire organisation and the way we operated, and the conclusion might be drawn from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. If you do not wish to talk about that, then the Trial Chamber might ask for a closed or private session, and then you might say who was giving you instructions, because that's important for my next question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: In what sense of the word do you mean "instructions"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I mean the instructions to set up the intercept group at the northern location and for it to begin working, because at that time the work in all locations around the Eagle Base was prohibited by the USA, and you were not allowed to locate units there unless they agreed or approved of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go into private session, if there's going to be any names of the people mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think that is appropriate. We go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we all would be pleased if you answered the question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness come closer to the microphones, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You probably know from all this that we were so short of troops and so short of resources that it never occurred to us to listen to the conversations that you just mentioned. That is to say, we couldn't properly control what was the subject of wartime conflict and what was really the subject of our interest. I already talked earlier today about the subject of our interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know that on the Serbian side, such a location in the so-called place Vis was bombed from the Eagle Base because of the same activities that you were engaging in? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me, then, what you do know. Were you allowed to record activities and intercept conversations of the BH Army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: We were not doing that. Let me just recall very briefly that we only had two men in one shift. If you take that into account and see how much work we did, you will see that these two men couldn't do anything more than what they did do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you ever requested to record a unit that was in your surrounding area or in enemy territory that had nothing to do with your corps, so that you would provide information to the corps about the location of this unit and whether they were all safe and sound, or did you ever establish connection with that unit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: You have asked me many questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please answer just one question.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I never received any instructions or orders from the corps because I was not a part of any military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether the Ministry of Defence was part of the Ministry of the Interior and the Armed Forces of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you obliged to carry out all orders that you received from the Supreme Command or the chief of Supreme Command, because he was military personnel, he was a member of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me, but you are very well familiar with the organisation. So this is civilian military service. I could only be issued orders by my direct superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please say, for the needs of the Trial Chamber and the transcript, whether your ministry was part of the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the ministry for which you worked?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, it was so. I already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right, thank you. But I had to ask you that because you keep talking about the civilian service, civilian intelligence service. I had to know if this was a civilian service or if it was an integral part of the armed forces. I apologise once again, and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask a question at this point in time, Mr. Tolimir. I think to clarify this structure, I would like to know if the State Security Service you were talking about was part of the Ministry of Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, at the time it was an integral part of the Ministry of Interior, which had the Public Security Sector and the State Security Sector or Department, so it had two sectors or departments, and we were the State Security Department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Ministry of Defence was a separate ministry, is that correct, or was there a link to the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the war, we all were considered members of the army, regardless of the structure to which we belonged. We are recording as having been members of the armed forces during the war, but we were the service that we were. How that was decided, I wouldn't know. And we were not uniformed members of the army, and our duties were civilian ones, so in that sense we were not members of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was not my question. I would like to know the relation between the Ministry of Interior and the Ministry of Defence. Are they separate ministries, or was one of these ministries part of the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, these were separate ministries within one single government, the Ministry of the Interior, on the one hand, and the Ministry of Defence, on the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand. I did ask this question because on page 59, lines 5 through 7, you were asked by Mr. Tolimir: "Can you tell me whether the Ministry of Defence was part of the Ministry of the Interior and the Armed Forces of the BH Army?" And then you answered: "Yes, it did."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he made the question complicated. What I said later is true. During the war, the Ministry of the Interior was an integral part of the armed forces and not an integral part of the Ministry of Defence. So the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of the Interior had two ministers, and these were two separate ministries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. There's another question by Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: At page 59, lines 3 and 4, you've stated that: "I never received any instructions or orders from the corps because I was not a part of the military unit." Can you explain exactly how you fit into the structure and from whom you got your orders.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received all orders from the chief of the State Security Service and its department in Tuzla. The facilities where I were [as interpreted] were assigned to us for practical reasons, because during one shift I only had two men at my disposal. It was at a distant location, at an elevation. For two men to work, they need security, they need other elements of logistics as well. That was why we asked for one room to be assigned to us, where we could work independently, and there were no uniformed people there except at the moment when information was exchanged. We used floppy discs at the time. So apart from us, the facilities were used by the PEB of the 2nd Corps, but we were independent of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: How independent were you within this unit? For example, how would you decide -- maybe let me rephrase my question. How were your assignments given to you? How did you decide what to pass on to the military or to whoever among the intercepts that you handled, since you say you were an independent structure within the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't say we were an independent structure. We are now talking only about the facility in this location and about us. When we began to receive information from intercepts, we realised that it was very practical to pass on the information that had to do with military operations to the army, and they also had information that we could use. So we reached an internal agreement to exchange all information, because in this way we wouldn't cause any harm to anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Another question by Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said earlier, but I can't find the page right now, that when you would receive military -- very important military information, you would, of course, send this information to the military personnel, but that your work consisted in getting information and sending that information to the civil, civilian structures. Could you please give me some examples of information that were more civilian information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can give you such information. For example, most of the conversations in which Mr. Krajisnik or Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Koljevic participated were such. I think that is sufficient, but there was quite a lot of other information as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So when you talk about civilian information, you talk about political information; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Civilian authorities, civilian structures, relation to certain events, and other things that might be interesting; also, what was the atmosphere among the people, the civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. I understand better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir. Apologies for these interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell me whether intercepting the enemy army and wire-tapping the enemy army is a civilian duty, as you just described these activities to us? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: We intercepted everything, anything that we could hear. There could be no selection, because that was information that you received in your ear. So we could not skip information that told us that a certain area would be shelled, even though it was military information. Therefore -- please let me finish. At the same time, if shells were fired on a certain area, we would be interested in learning whether the population in your area reacted; when they received information in the media that a certain number of people were killed, just as an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would ask you that later and I would ask for additional time, because I only have a little time left. So if you want to continue, then you would have an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: No, I have finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I only wish to ask you this: Were you assigned a room because of civilian -- even though these were military facilities, did you receive that as civilians?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, we were allowed to receive what was important for us, but I also added just a little while ago that we couldn't skip over the information that were important for the army and then pass on to the army. That was quite normal, just like the army, if it got hold of information that were important for the work of the State Security Service, it would submit the information to us. You know that it's normal work, especially in wartime conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Can you please tell me, when you registered a conversation by foreign people, how did you know that these were not military activities? Because you told us that you would take this to be translated. Were there any such conversations that you registered? Because an intercept device has to register all the conversations that are received.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: We were listening to your radio-relay communication channels, we were listening to you, and in these channels, very often -- I'm not sure how many times, but very often we heard conversations of your officials who were using interpreters because they were talking with English-speaking persons, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't have to explain. Can you just answer the question. I'm asking short questions, and there will be questions to which you will be able to answer as you wish. Thank you. Now please tell me, as you said in examination-in-chief that there were communications problems and that you would use dots, which you also said during your earlier testimony in the Popovic case, can you then tell me, please, if you were using an adequate antenna or whether you had to adapt it so that your reception would be better?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: We were using an adequate antenna, but there were some signals that we could not hear well at all. So when we could just hear a little bit from these signals with a professional military antenna, we tried to find a better solution, and so we set up the parabolic antenna so that we would receive maximum audibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could this parabolic antenna record conversations lower than 1 gigahertz? Because you said during your examination-in-chief that it was meant to be used for the range of frequencies between 600 and 900 megahertz. Please answer briefly.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: We were using the antenna which we received for the radio-relay channel and for the range of frequencies that we could listen to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you saying that a parabolic antenna was able to receive signals lower than 1 gigahertz? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: In this specific case, I was not trying to do calculations about the antenna. But when I was requesting assistance to resolve the issue, I received an antenna for which I was told that it had been used for a specific radio-relay channel that had been inactive, so they took off this antenna and then they set it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand everything now. Can you tell me who was the chief of the centre that your group was part of?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: You want me to mention the name?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If the person's name is secret, you don't have to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: It's not secret, but I'm not sure, because a name occurs now -- it's not secret. It's something that is general knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please ask the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, can the Prosecutor please state what I should do? I don't know. I think that it wouldn't be good if I was to mention names in open session. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can assist by -- these issues, as you can imagine, are very sensitive to the governments involved. And I would appreciate it, and as I think the general has understood, that anybody's name in these services should be mentioned in private session. You will be hearing from -- other intercepts from other countries where we will get the briefest of information, for security reasons. So we're getting quite a bit of information, but if we could, just out of an abundance of caution, have the supervisors' and the other people's names under seal, that would be a very good idea. This war is still an issue in the country, as you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And now, Witness, could you please answer the question of Mr. Tolimir. We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You asked about the chief of my service in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The accused did not switch his microphone off. We cannot hear the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His name was Pasaga Mesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I was not interested in functionaries. You told us that you were a part of the Intelligence and Security Service of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: The State Security Service in a country is common knowledge, it's the civilian intelligence service of a country. I don't know what else to tell you. Is my understanding of your question correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and it is a follow-up to what you earlier on said. You said that you -- your duties were of a civilian nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, overlapping. It's the first point. And the other is, we are still in private session. Is there any further need for that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need for that. I wanted to ask the witness about this, but he refuses to answer. Well, I thought this was a problem because he felt that the name of his chief was confidential too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you intend asking for more names?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't intend to ask for more names. I'm merely asking the witness to tell me what the character of his institution was, and that's why I asked him what his superior was. And, of course, I want to go back to public session because this is not a secret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Public.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in public session, if you were the component part of the Intelligence and Security Services --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we are in open session, but you should continue after the second break. This is, I think, the convenient time for everybody to have the second break, and then you may continue your questioning. We will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you may carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, a moment ago you said that you belonged to the security and intelligence structure and that you gathered intelligence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do security and intelligence matters fall under civilian or military activities?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, they can be both.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that you intercepted other matters as well. Can you tell us, what are these other matters? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: We intercepted all the conversations that we assessed as possibly useful in our work. The extent to which information could be used and their actual value was not something that we assessed. This was assessed by the individuals who received the information from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I only wanted to know what these other matters were, and not what their value was. Can you tell us, did you keep in touch with the radio amateurs in Srebrenica and the troops there?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: As far as that location is concerned, we only intercepted the waves transmitted along the radio-relay route, and in general terms we intercepted the communications of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And which other sites or stations of yours kept in touch with Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: It was a different location in a different period of time. It was, in fact, a detached communications centre of this service, and it has nothing to do with the matters we are discussing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did you at any point in time record any sort of information related to the forces of the BH Army in the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, is it possible to adjust the equipment so as to intercept only the information related to the adversary and not the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible to do so. You know that this was the sole subject of our interest. I know that you have a great deal of knowledge on this issue. You will, therefore, understand why I accept these questions of yours in this way. We scanned the entire frequency range, and the specialist told us which of these frequencies were used by both the army and some of the civilian telephone lines, and we did this as well. You have to keep in mind the fact that we were short of staff. We only had two individuals doing the job, and you will realise that it was impossible for them to do all the matters that you refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As a follow-up to my earlier question, did the device have the possibility to make a selection and distinguish between the conversations taking place on the opposite side and the conversations taking place on your side?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, it could. The radio-relay link that we listened in to was the one that was solely used by the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this device automatically exclude all other participants in conversations, or was this something that had to be done manually?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I don't know if we understand each other correctly. If we are listening to the frequency, say, 785, this is a frequency solely used by you, and therefore it would not have any other conversations taking part there, like conversations, for instance, of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please pause. You are overlapping, both of you, at the moment. Please pause and then continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please answer this question of mine. Was it possible to have a conversation taking place on the frequency that you were listening to which involved members of the BH Army from the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I think that it was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you intercepted conversations, the participants of which were only members of the VRS, did you also intercept conversations that they had with UNPROFOR troops?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I do recall one, two, three, or five - I don't know how many - conversations where an interpreter was used. Now, who was at the other end, well, I know of this one case, and I can't recall others. But I do know there were conversations taking place in the English language.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, did you enter these conversations into your log-book, the one that was showed to you a moment ago when the OTP representative asked you of the meaning of the various columns there?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I think that this is a good question. Since the assistance of an interpreter was required, I do recall this one occasion when we took along an interpreter to the location where we worked. There was a possibility, however, that a tape containing such a recording of such a conversation would be taken to the head office of the service, where it would be translated. In that case, the intercept would be entered into the log-book of the head office. But I'm talking about exceptions, of course. I do recall one intercept having been translated up there, and then there was one other case where either the translator was absent or unable to come, so it was translated elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, does the log-book contain intercepts of conversations between representatives of the Serb side and English-speaking interlocutors?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are we going to be able to recognise it? Will you be able to recognise it in the log-book by looking at the numbers?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I can't recognise a single intercept in the log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago, you said that sometimes you had to reconstruct portions of conversations and that sometimes you would also call an interpreter to come to your location in order to help you. Was the selection done by you, by your better judgement, as to what it is that should be forwarded to your superior and what shouldn't? Because, of course, first of all, you had to understand what it was about.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Again, you've put several questions to me. First of all, we did not reconstruct conversations in any way. I explained that if we heard a conversation taking place in English, we would not try and grasp the meaning. We would rather call for an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: A moment ago, during the examination-in-chief, you said that you produced a note or a transcription of the intercept on paper, which would be typed up in a computer and then the paper would be destroyed. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: You didn't put the question to me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you then tell me what the procedure was?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Can you please put shorter questions to me? We didn't create a note. It was a transcription of the conversation which contained everything that I mentioned; participants, time, frequency, channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You also said that the operator would note it down on paper and that there were some portions of the conversation that he wouldn't be able to hear, or that the recording wouldn't start in time, that the conversation was already ongoing when the recording started, and then parts of the conversation would be missed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases where you would hear, for instance, you picking up a receiver and saying, Tolimir speaking. Can I talk to Marko? And by the time the operator heard this, he would switch the button on for recording, but by that time he would have missed -- he wouldn't be able to record the beginning. But the operator would, nevertheless, use the information in writing down that the conversation was taking place between Tolimir and Marko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can this be a document used before a court of law if the document indicates that the person intercepting the conversation had a clear idea of who the interlocutors were, but that it doesn't transpire from the transcription?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Well, it's up to the Trial Chamber to decide this. And I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I stopped you because again it is impossible for the interpreters to catch what you are talking about. Look at the transcript and wait that the sentence is recorded to the end. And now continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The transcript is in English, and we are both of us speaking Serbian, but we will try to comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please answer this question briefly, if you remember it. If not, I'll repeat it.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were there any cases where the operators, the listeners, arbitrarily interpret some content or part of content which is not distinctly audible and cannot be transcribed on paper?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: There were cases where, from one voice content, you are able to understand the meaning of what is said. It was not a form of transcription. It is written down precisely as I'm trying to explain; namely, that in a part of the conversation, there was reference to shelling. What was being shelled and where could not be heard, but the gist of the reference was clear, and that's the way the operator would note it down. He would not try to put it in the mouth of any of the speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were those intercepts that you recorded kept safeguarded, where are they kept, and where can we find these recordings that you recorded on the UHER device?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: If you listened to me carefully, I have spoken in my evidence about this. I meant to continue. I'm trying to follow the typing. Our job was to finish this technical work. We would then hand it over to other people who are in charge, as operative officers, of the rest of the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But tell me, did you, and I mean you personally, have, in safekeeping, any of this material on site at the location where you were working, or did you have it kept elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: In that period, among other things, in a safe box at the communications centre, the transcripts were kept. Now, it has all been handed over further on by the communications centre, so there's nothing there anymore. Now, when the -- let me try to explain. When the communication centre receives this and they print it out, they pass it on to the chief, and the transcripts were recorded on floppy discs and they were kept for a while in the safe box. I know this for a fact. Now, when this was transferred to the people who were responsible for that work, I don't know exactly, but it was towards the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you were not sure. You don't know whether it has been kept to date, I mean, the magnetic tapes?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: At this moment, I don't know where they are or how many they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you answer this question: If you listened to a communication in a network and there was several conversations, did you select conversations to intercept, or did you record all of them and then later transcribe them?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: There were persons -- there were personalities, rather, whose all conversations we recorded, and there were other communication lines that we monitored. And occasionally we would come upon a conversation that we would later find irrelevant, and then we would tape it over --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, how much time passed between your receipt of information on your devices and the time when it was received by the end user.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: That depended. If something was very important, it would be transcribed immediately and passed on immediately. And you can see that from these reports, and I can show you in my log-book, the log-book of files sent. You will see that there are, for instance, conversations recorded at 8.20 and passed on at 9.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said something very important. Concerning such very important things, did you preserve the recording of the conversation, and where would it be?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Again, I've said this in my previous evidence. If we estimated that something was very important, there was one tape on which we recorded or dubbed these very important conversations, but we didn't have the time or the men to do all this. But I know there are recordings for everything. Once something is evaluated as very important, we would dub it on that special tape, and we would mark the time, and we would mark the participants in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We discussed a very important conversation in the past exchange. Tell us, what is the purpose of intercepting conversations in a certain radio network, and why is this information important?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Simply, it's important because it's gathering intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible -- is the possibility of quick conveyance of information very important in interception?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is the speed with which you forward information from your interception centre to the user an important factor in your work?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Depending on the content of information, the speed is sometimes very important. Other types of information can wait a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the Popovic trial, page 6124, lines 3 through 6, you said: "We did not keep the papers on which we transcribed conversations. We burnt them as soon as we have passed on our messages to the centre office." So you decided yourself what you would keep, what you would not, what would be documented, what would not?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: We did not decide that. After we transcribed a conversation and after we re-typed it into the computer, we thought this paper was superfluous and dangerous to keep on the intercepting site, and that's why we destroyed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked you this because you said this note-book would soon be received by us. I'm interested, is it possible to find this note-book where you actually transcribed conversations? Because in another trial, you said, We burnt papers as soon as we sent our information to the head office. That's written on the page I indicated, 6124, lines 3 to 6.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I will try to explain this distinction. The papers on which we wrote down the conversations, after they were typed on the computer and passed on to the centre, we disposed of the paper and burnt it. Now, this agenda book where we recorded all the files sent to the centre is something different. We don't have it here right now, but we could have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the intercepts that you wrote down in hand get burned as soon as you received feedback that they had been received at your head office?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: That's not right. The device we used to transmit these files always gave a confirmation of receipt, and we were always sure that everything was received. So it had nothing to do with the destruction of paper. We had electronic confirmation that messages were received. People down there would type it out or, rather, print it out and pass it on. And after that, we destroyed our papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm not asking anything for my own benefit. I know very well how it works. But you said in the Popovic transcript, page 6124, I quote: "We did not keep the papers on which we transcribed conversations. We burnt them as soon as we have sent messages to our head office." Did I quote this correctly?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Quite possibly I put it that way, but whether I burnt it that same second or I waited a day or two is not important, in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said in examination-in-chief here, and in the Popovic case as well, that sometimes, and I quote document 1D160, page 3, para 3, lines 9 to 12; in English, it's page 3, para 3, lines 9 through 11 -- while we're waiting for that to appear on the screen, I'll quote to you what you said, because we have no time. I quote: "Sometimes we paraphrased the conversation, but we did that in peculiar, particular circumstances. For instance, if a reporter from Republika Srpska was passing on this information, we usually did not transcribe such conversations, but would summarise them." Did I quote you correctly?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: You did, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is that authentic, this paraphrasing you engaged in sometimes? Would your summaries also be authentic, based on your listening to conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: If you just remember what you said, a reporter -- a radio reporter, we heard a radio reporter who was reporting radio news that would be broadcast the same evening, and the piece of news was full of false information, and that was two full pages. So we thought that we could summarise it so that we wouldn't transcribe it in full, as it did not have any special weight. These were radio reporters of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I have understood you very well, because conversations from the media are sometimes quoted here in the trials. This is my following question: Who in your group was the one whose duty was to paraphrase such intercepted conversations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: If you allow me to say something briefly. This was intelligence information. The same information was broadcast on the TV news of Republika Srpska from Pale. It is something that the Court and everyone else can find, and then you can compare how we paraphrased the information. You know that better than I do, if I may say so. You know that such news, such information in the war, does not have the weight of information as spoken by Karadzic, Mladic, or someone else. This is the way the journalists would formulate it in the media. We would assess that we should our superiors about it and that it had that particular content, but we just wouldn't want to type out two full pages because it would be broadcast the same evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Who would paraphrase and adapt such intercepts so that they would be such news so that you would send them to the final users?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Please don't say that they were adapted. The truth is the only important thing here. No one had the right to -- no one had the right to spin such news, because we didn't try to paint a nice picture of anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Then can you tell me who paraphrased what you heard in the intercepted conversation and that you then forwarded to your head office as information or as your report? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: It was suggested to all operators that when they heard media reports or information, something that was unimportant or that the context was such that because of poor audibility, one might only conclude what the context was, that that should be noted, but everything else is explained in the transcript; when persons are called X or Y instead of with their name, when there were dots, and so on. But what you want to tell me now was that I was sending this information to my own superiors, and that was not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. I have listened to you, but please be even more brief in your answers because we only have 20 minutes left. I just wanted to ask you whether the meaning of the message would disappear because of the paraphrasing that you used. And were you only talking about media reports or about the sources that you were intercepting? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I think that you are wasting your time. These were media reporters whom we managed to hear when they were conveying information. That is what we paraphrased, or, rather, not paraphrased, but we would just make a note saying that the reporter was reporting about such and such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please tell the Court what was the frequency 83600, what radio network was that, and what could you hear from it, if you remember? If you don't, please just say so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I remember. That was the frequency on which we had 24 channels. Of the 24 channels, I remember well that channel number 13 was the channel used by General Mladic. As for the others, there were others where we could hear Mr. Koljevic or Mr. Krajisnik. This is what I know for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that General Mladic was on that channel all the time? Was it a channel that belonged to him and that he was using? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: That is not correct. He was not in his office all the time, and the evidence of that is the earlier transcript, because he appeared on frequency 785 during the incidents in Srebrenica. So he left his office, and he now communicated through another radio-relay communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, what was the frequency between Vlasenica and Zvornik, which you have mentioned? Can you tell us where and how it worked, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I talked about that. It was a radio-relay communication. I think it was 785.00 megahertz. But it was a long time ago, and please don't get me wrong if I don't remember something.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you answer my next question?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you know what were the locations of these radio-relay stations of the Army of Republika Srpska that you were monitoring? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I didn't know that. However, I received a map from the army on which they showed me and said, Look, here is Han Pijesak, here is Cer, here are Duge Njive, because I am not educated in this field, but I could understand it and I could use it. It was the army that dealt with this. I cannot hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please show 65 ter 2923. It's a prosecution document. Thank you. 65 ter 2923, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is Exhibit P239.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In this document, when you analysed it during examination-in-chief, you talked about what it stood for. If we look at the transcript now, in line 24 and onwards, was it recorded directly or was it paraphrased? I will quote what it says here: "We did not target civilians, but armed terrorists who had to be disarmed in accordance with our agreement which we signed in the presence of UN, and this was not done." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I cannot see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, he may be referring to one of the conversations that's not been translated because it was not one of the ones that we were interested in. I don't know, but that is my likely guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Tolimir, you were referring to a part of the transcript of today or another day or another trial. I'm not sure about that. What do you mean by "the transcript now, in line 24 and onwards"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, it's not a problem. Could we just show the documents from the note-book which was presented today during examination-in-chief. If we can show the documents one by one. Thank you. That is the document P239, or 65 ter 2923, and onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document is on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We can see one such document now. It's the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And you talk about communication between Zvornik and Vlasenica, and the frequency is 785. At 0822 hours, you registered a conversation between one Miro and an unidentified male person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is the portion at the top of this page which is not translated into English, but continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it generally known that on that day, at this time, civilians were being transported from Srebrenica, through Potocari, and into Kladanj in the vehicles that are mentioned here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Are you asking me whether that was really carried out on that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That's right, because the first part of the conversation mentions a vehicle which is towing a tank. Is that normal during armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot answer any of that. I don't know what was happening in the field. I did not see a tank during the war in any of the operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. If you did not see a tank, and you don't think a tank can be used in conflict --

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: No, no, I just didn't see one during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Then please answer another question. During examination-in-chief, you said that your signature on this document is marked with "1160" [as interpreted]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And then later you said that you did not register the names of other participants in the next conversation. That's number 557 which you can see on the screen, that you did not -- so you did not record the names of the participants, because the operator heard it, but by the time he could write it down and turn on the device, then the conversation could no longer be heard; is that correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The beginning could not be heard anymore when they introduced themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I talk about that, I'm talking in general terms. Whether it was me or somebody else --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please answer with yes or no, and then you might comment on that.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: I cannot do it without the comment. I said that this was happening. I was one of the operators at the moment, but I didn't remember every conversation, nor could I do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you could not identify the participants in the conversations. When you recorded it, you couldn't say who it was. Thank you. We're reading the conversation number 557 which you transcribed in the computer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Are you going to read it or what? I'm not sure what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Just for the Court, only one of the participants is named here, and that's Mr. Ognjenovic. The other one is not identified, so one can just suppose who it was. Is that correct or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: You can see for yourself that he's not identified, but he is addressed as a general here. But which general it was, it never says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Now I'm asking you this: Can it be an authentic document if someone is to be charged or believed to be responsible when there are so many generals in any given army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-024: Ferid MUSLIĆ
utterances.text: Do you really think that I can answer such a question? In the context of a series of other reports, can this be something you can be charged with or not, how could I say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm just asking you, because you said that you personally registered this conversation and entered it into the computer. Did you also burn the notes, on the basis of which you determined that such and such a conversation was conducted at such and such a time and on the basis of which you entered that into the computer from the handwritten notes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to indicate that this is the last question for today, but we would like to listen to the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who burned this piece of paper. It was not important for us at all. I did register this, I did record it, I did say that this was a general, but not General so-and-so, because I did not hear the name, and I think that everything is clear about that. No one had the right to say, General so-and-so, even though it could happen that according to some other information, one might conclude that only General Krstic was in this particular area. But one couldn't record that because he was not addressed by his name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you, Witness. If you appear in the courtroom again, I will ask you to be more brief in your answers so that we could finish as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you could also try to ask simple questions and try not to ask three questions within one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, thank you. I wish to thank the Presiding Judge, and the interpreters, and everyone else who participated in this process. And I thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we are really running out of time. If I understood the scheduling list, this witness will be available tomorrow for continuation of the cross-examination. Is that correct, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and there is an army witness after that. Could we get an estimate so that the witness people could start planning for that and we can plan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That would be helpful, Mr. Tolimir. What is the estimation of time you need?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have another 30 questions. I can read out the 30 questions. If I read them, I need 15 minutes, but it depends on the answers given by the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your time estimation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My estimate, considering, though, the length of answers, is that I would need approximately one session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That would be much more than you indicated earlier, that you would need one hour and thirty minutes. That is perhaps a little bit too long, and you should discuss it with your legal advisor if you can perhaps shorten this time. We have to adjourn now. But before we do that, I have to let you know that we have a change in the sitting time for tomorrow. This courtroom -- there's a need for another Trial Chamber to use this courtroom in the early morning, until 10.00, so that we have to start a little bit later, at 10.30, until 3.15 in the afternoon. This is the normal time, but postponed for one and a half hours. We adjourn now and resume tomorrow at 10.30 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 28th day of May, 2010, at 10.30 a.m. 24 25
